title: The sea every morning (Exodus 15)
hookLine: the verses of song end with the Song of the Sea, sung daily

cards: A people who were slaves the week before stand on the far shore of a sea. Behind them, the water has closed. Ahead, the desert, and no idea what comes next.
They crossed on dry ground, and they're exhausted, terrified and alive. And they sing. Moses sings, the people sing with him, and Miriam takes a drum while the women dance.

Many scholars count it among the oldest poems in the Bible. Every morning, at the very end of the verses of song, Jews who pray the full service sing it again, as if they'd just stepped onto that shore.

teach.h: SHIRAT HAYAM: THE SONG OF THE SEA.
teach.b: It's called Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea, from Exodus fifteen. In the old Jewish translation it begins: "I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea."
Then a line that turns up all over Jewish prayer: "The LORD is my strength and song." Even the way it's written is different. In a Torah scroll, this song isn't laid out in plain columns.

teach.h: WRITTEN LIKE A WALL OF BRICKS.
teach.b: The Talmud describes it as half bricks over whole bricks: short lines and gaps staggered like a wall, so you can spot it from across the room. The opening words are az yashir, then sang Moses.

teach.h: AZ YASHIR: SANG, OR WILL SING.
teach.b: But the Hebrew verb can also be read as will sing, and the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, hears a hint that the song isn't over, that it will be sung again in a world to come.
Some commentators say to say it each morning with joy, as if you yourself had crossed that day. And there's a well-known counterweight.
The Talmud tells that when the Egyptians were drowning, the angels wanted to sing too, and God stopped them: the work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing?
Israel's song of rescue is kept, every morning. But the tradition remembers that the rescue had a cost, and that God grieves for every creature.

how: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 14:30–15:18) is said each morning near the end of the verses of song, often standing, and it is read from the Torah on the seventh day of Passover and on Shabbat Shirah.

games.q: you're an angel watching the sea close over the Egyptian army. Israel is singing on the shore. you want to join in. what happens?
o: God invites you to sing louder.
God stops you: my handiwork is drowning.
games.why: in the Talmud's telling, God silences the angels: the work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing? Israel's song is kept; the cost is remembered.

practice: Think of something you came through, an illness, a move, a loss, a terrible year, and picture yourself on its far shore.

Then sing one line aloud, even softly, even off-key: ozi v'zimrat Yah, the LORD is my strength and song, if you know it, or a song you love if you don't. Let it go quiet, and remember someone who didn't make it through with you.
